query: Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys have reported densities of 1.46–6 g/cm3 and commonly contain solid solutions together with intermetallic compounds. Earlier induction-melted Al–Mg-rich alloys established this structural complexity but did not resolve subsequent transformation pathways. Compositionally graded MgAlCuZnGd alloys showed region-dependent compression and corrosion performance, while studies of AlMgₓTiSnZn alloys associated Mg content with phase stability and multiple functional properties. Most prior work emphasized hardness and room-temperature compression, leaving corrosion, high-temperature oxidation, and evolution from metastable states comparatively underexplored. Within the design constraint of density below 6 g/cm3 and the tendency for constituent-property differences to promote stable intermetallic compounds, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain how a non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy evolves and why that evolution changes its corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior? Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predictions relative to the initial baseline, boundary conditions, supporting prior observations, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In non‐equilibrium Mg‐containing lightweight high‐entropy alloys (HEAs), the initial metastable microstructure—characterized by a BCC (or similar) solid solution with fine Mg‐rich intermetallic precipitates—evolves during thermal and corrosive exposure through coarsening and Mg segregation at grain boundaries. This microstructural change promotes the formation of porous, non‐adherent Mg‐rich oxide layers that accelerate high‐temperature oxidation and corrosion relative to the initial state.
generation.material_initial_state: A metastable, non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight HEA (density below 6 g/cm³) with a homogeneous distribution of a primary solid solution (likely BCC) and nanometer-scale Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates.
generation.intervention: Subject the alloy to elevated temperatures (e.g., ≥800 °C for oxidation tests) or prolonged exposure in corrosive environments (e.g., saline solution) to trigger microstructural evolution.
generation.conditions: High-temperature exposure conditions (with dwell times sufficient to allow precipitate coarsening) and controlled corrosive environments that simulate long-term operational conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Coarsening and loss of coherency of the fine Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates along with the consequent segregation of Mg to grain boundaries and phase interfaces.
generation.mechanism: Thermal activation increases atomic diffusion, causing the initially fine Mg-rich precipitates to coarsen and lose their coherent relationship with the matrix. This promotes the segregation of Mg at microstructural discontinuities, facilitating the preferential formation of Mg-oxide phases that are porous and less adherent. The non-protective nature of these oxide films increases both oxidation rates at high temperatures and susceptibility to corrosive attack.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples that have been thermally or corrosively aged will exhibit a visibly coarsened and segregated microstructure, with enhanced thickness and porosity of Mg-rich oxide scales, leading to an increase in high-temperature oxidation rates (e.g., higher weight gain per unit area) and accelerated corrosion compared to the as-cast metastable baseline.
generation.baseline: The as-processed, metastable microstructure with finely dispersed Mg-rich precipitates uniformly embedded within a solid-solution matrix.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to Mg-containing lightweight HEAs with densities below 6 g/cm³ and significant compositional inhomogeneity (i.e., presence of metastable intermetallic phases). Alloys outside this compositional or processing window may exhibit different evolution pathways.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative extent of precipitate coarsening, the exact kinetics of Mg segregation, and their direct correlation with oxide scale porosity are not yet established and require systematic investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare Mg-containing lightweight HEA samples using identical processing conditions to achieve the initial metastable state. Divide the samples into two groups: a control group maintained at room temperature and a test group subjected to high-temperature exposure (≥800 °C) and/or immersion in a 3.5 wt% NaCl solution for extended periods. Before and after exposure, characterize the microstructure using transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) to assess precipitate size, distribution, and Mg segregation at grain boundaries. Additionally, perform thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) to quantify oxidation kinetics and electrochemical corrosion tests (e.g., Tafel analysis) to determine corrosion rates.
measurements: Precipitate size distribution and coherence with the matrix (TEM)
Mg concentration profiles at grain boundaries (EDS mapping)
Oxide scale thickness, porosity, and composition (SEM/EDS, XRD)
Weight gain per unit area during high-temperature oxidation (TGA)
Corrosion potential and corrosion rate in saline solution (potentiodynamic polarization)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If, after exposure, there is no significant coarsening of the Mg-rich precipitates or Mg segregation at grain boundaries, and the resulting oxide scales are similar in structure and protective quality to those of the as-processed state—resulting in no measurable increase in oxidation kinetics or corrosion rate compared to the control—then the hypothesis is falsified.

Question: How can high-throughput computational screening be used to discover lightweight, precipitation-strengthened high-entropy alloys with high-temperature strength superior to traditional ferritic superalloys?. System: Al–Cr–Fe–Mn–Ti quinary system (specifically Al20Cr5Fe50Mn20Ti5 and Al15Cr5Fe50Mn25Ti5 as successful cases). Processing: Arc-melting of 99.9 wt% purity constituent elements, melted at least six times for homogeneity, followed by drop-casting; subsequent homogenization at 1200 °C and annealing at 700 °C for 2 hours for specific characterizations. Test conditions: Compression tests at room temperature and elevated temperatures (up to 700 °C) at a strain rate of 2 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹; in situ neutron scattering from room temperature to 1050 °C; synchrotron XRD and TEM characterization.
